pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/ˈdɑːrmə/** ​— ​Sanskrit (IAST: ‌Dharma).[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

- ​**Dhar-** — ‌The ​dh ‌is ​a ​voiced aspirate ​— ​“d” ​with ‌breath; ​the a ‌is ​long ‌“ah”.
- ​**-ma** ‌— The ​word ‌is ​the ​abstract ‌noun ‌from √dhṛ, ‌“to ​hold, ​sustain” ‌— ​that which ​holds ‌the ​world ​up.

‌For the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ​approximation is: ​“DAHR-muh”

‌Kindred ‌and ​historical ‌forms of ​the ​name:

- ‌**Pāli** ‌— ‌Dhamma
- ‌**Avestan** — ​daēnā ‌(cognate ​family)

​Not ​a god ‌but ​a ​principle ​— ‌personified as ​a ​god ​in ‌the ​epics, whence ‌this ​entry. ‌In ​compounds ‌the stem ‌appears ​as ​dharma-; ​Middle ​Indic shortens ‌it ‌to ​dhamma-.

domains.body:
**Dharma** ​is the ‌load-bearing word ‌of Indian ​civilization: ​the law ​that holds ​the ​cosmos, the ‌duty that ​holds the ​person, ‌the order ​that holds ‌society. ​From √dhṛ, ‌‘to sustain’, ​it names ​everything ​that keeps ​the world ​from ‌sliding into ​chaos — ‌and in ​the ‌epics it ​walks as ‌a ​person: the ‌god of ​righteousness, father ​of ‌Yudhiṣṭhira, who ‌came down ‌to ​test his ​own devotees.[^1]

### ‌The Load-Bearer

​The ​cosmos rests ‌on dharma; ​the ​four feet ‌of the ​bull of ‌dharma ​mark the ​four ages ​of ​time.

### Duty ‌by Caste ‌and Stage

​Svadharma ‌— one’s ​own duty ​by ‌birth and ‌life-stage: the ‌Bhagavadgītā’s central ‌teaching.

### ​The Cosmic ‌Ages

The ​four ​yugas are ​the four ‌feet of ​the ​bull: four ​in the ‌Kṛta ​age, one ​stumbling foot ​in ours.

### ‌The ​Tester of ‌Men

In ​the ‌epics Dharma ​appears in ‌disguise — ‌a ​beggar, a ​dog, a ​crane ​— to ‌test righteousness ‌where it ​counts.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Dharma ​concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about the ​name:[^1]

- ‌**The ​Load-Bearer** ​— The ​cosmos ​rests ​on ‌dharma; the ​four ‌feet ​of ‌the bull ​of ‌dharma ​mark ‌the four ​ages ​of ‌time.
- ‌**Duty by ‌Caste ​and ​Stage** ‌— Svadharma ​— ​one’s ‌own ​duty by ​birth ‌and ​life-stage: ‌the Bhagavadgītā’s ​central ​teaching.
- ​**The ​Cosmic Ages** ‌— ‌The ​four ‌yugas are ​the ​four ‌feet ‌of the ‌bull: ‌four ​in ‌the Kṛta ​age, ​one ​stumbling ‌foot in ​ours.
- ​**The ​Tester ‌of Men** ​— ​In ​the ‌epics Dharma ​appears ‌in ​disguise ‌— a ​beggar, ‌a ‌dog, ​a crane ​— ​to ​test ‌righteousness where ‌it ​counts.

mythology.body:
Dharma’s mythology ​is the epics’ moral ‌machinery: the god ‌of righteousness fathers ​the eldest Pāṇḍava, tests ​his devotees in ​disguise, and — in ​the Nala story ​— teaches dice ‌to a king as ​the instrument of ​ruin. He has ‌no cult-image because he ​is what every ‌cult-image stands for; yet ​the tradition gave ‌him a family ​and a biography.[^1]

### The ​Father of Yudhiṣṭhira ​(Mahābhārata)

When Pāṇḍu was ​cursed to die ​on his wedding ‌night, his queens invoked ​the gods: Dharmarāja ‌himself, the god ​of righteousness, fathered Yudhiṣṭhira ‌on Kuntī. The ​eldest Pāṇḍava is thus ‌dharma’s son — ​which is why ‌the epic keeps asking ​whether righteousness itself ​can survive the dice-game ‌and the war ‌it forces.[^2]

### The ‌Tests in Disguise (Dharma-Upākhyāna)

​The epic’s forest-books ​stage Dharma’s examinations: ‌as a stork demanding ​why Yudhiṣṭhira would ​not abandon a fallen ‌brother; as a ​Yakṣa whose riddles ​the king answers with ‌the epic’s most ​quoted verses; as a ‌dog who follows ​the Pāṇḍavas to ​heaven’s gate and is ​refused entry — ​until Yudhiṣṭhira refuses heaven ‌without it. The ‌dog was Dharma; ​the gate opens.

### The ‌God Who Taught ​Dice (Nala Cycle)

​In the Nala episode, ‌Kali — the ‌demon of the Kali ‌Yuga — begs ‌Dharma for a ​means to enter the ‌righteous king Nala; ​Dharma, inexplicably, teaches him ​dice. The story’s ​commentators wrestled for ‌centuries with the god ​of righteousness arming ​the demon of ​strife: the standard resolution ‌— even dharma’s ​permission is a test ​that righteousness must ​survive.

### The Son ‌of Brahmā (Purāṇic Personification)

​The Purāṇas give ‌Dharma genealogy: born of ​Brahmā’s breast as ‌one of the ​mind-born sons, husband of ‌Dhṛti and father ‌of the personified ​virtues — Kāma (desire), ​Lobha (greed), Darpa ​(pride) and the rest. ​The abstraction’s family-tree ‌is the Indian ‌psyche’s map of its ​own forces.

sources.citation: Purāṇic genealogies of the mind-born sons.

overview.body:
**Dharma** (*dharma*) ​— That ‌Which Holds, ‌Law and ​Righteousness · ​That which ​holds or ​sustains — ​law, duty, ‌and righteousness ​— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Law, Duty, ​Righteousness". The ​name means ​"That which ​holds or ​sustains — ‌law, duty, ​and righteousness; ‌the moral ​and religious order ‌that upholds ​the world ‌(from √dhṛ, ​'to hold, ‌sustain')."[^1].

**Dharma** ​is the ​load-bearing word ‌of Indian ‌civilization: the ‌law that ​holds the ​cosmos, the ‌duty that holds ​the person, ​the order ‌that holds ​society. From ​√dhṛ, ‘to ‌sustain’, it ​names everything ‌that keeps ​the world ​from sliding ​into chaos ​— and in ‌the epics ‌it walks ​as a ‌person: the ​god of ​righteousness, father ‌of Yudhiṣṭhira, ‌who came ‌down to ‌test his ​own devotees.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ​the canonical scholarly ​spelling **Dharma** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/dharma/). The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed form ​itself. The plain ‌ASCII form ​*dharma* contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ‌or special ​encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ‌citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Devanagari ​as ​**धर्म**. Etymologically ​it ​means "That ​which ‌holds or ​sustains ​— ‌law, duty, ​and ‌righteousness; the ​moral ‌and religious ​order ​that upholds ​the ​world (from ​√dhṛ, ‌'to hold, ​sustain')."[^1].

‌The canonical ​spelling ‌**Dharma** matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form *dharma* ‌contains ‌the ‌same letters, ​so ​no lost ‌diacritics ​or encoding ​transition ‌is claimed. ​The ​editorial work ‌is ​to fix ‌one ​reviewed reference ​spelling, ​preserve capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ‌keep ​the original ‌evidence ​visible. ​The displayed ‌form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ‌a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed ​form itself.

- ​**d** → ​**D** ‌— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**h** → ​**h** ‌— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ‌Same
